extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent owners, petitioners, and USPTO staff (participants in AIA trial proceedings)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory rules and operational standards implementing inter partes review (IPR), post-grant review (PGR), and the transitional covered business method (CBM) review proceedings under the AIA, including filing, institution, practitioner qualifications, fees, timelines, and related procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of externally claimed apparatus (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significantly claimed apparatus external to this class, claimed in combination with apparatus under the class definition, which perform data processing or calculation operations are classified in the class appropriate to the external device unless specifically excluded therefrom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparatus that are external to Class 705 but claimed in combination with items under Class 705 are placed in the class appropriate to the external device unless that external class specifically excludes them. See Classification Definitions (Feb. 2011) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nominally claimed external apparatus (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominally claimed apparatus external to this class in combination with apparatus under the class definition is classified in this class unless provided for in the appropriate external class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an external apparatus is only nominally claimed (i.e., incidental) in combination with apparatus that fall squarely within Class 705, classify in Class 705 unless the external class provides for classification there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of classification schedule/environment for searches
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the nature of the subject matter included herein, consideration of the classification schedule for the diverse art or environment is necessary for proper search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers and searchers must review relevant classification definitions and schedules (e.g., Class 705 and related classes) to ensure thorough search coverage across diverse technological environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical class for CBM patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents subject to covered business method patent review are anticipated to be typically classifiable in Class 705.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many CBM-eligible patents will be in Class 705, there will also be patents classified in other classes that qualify as covered business method patents; coordinate classification when determining CBM eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year final determination requirement (with limited extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director must prescribe rules so that an inter partes review, post-grant review, or covered business method patent review results in a final determination not later than one year after the date on which the Director notices the institution of a proceeding; the one-year period may be extended for not more than six months if good cause is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing requirement is grounded in 35 U.S.C. 316(a)(11) and 326(a)(11). Rules are designed to produce a final PTAB determination within one year except where good cause for an extension (up to 6 months) is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking considerations for Director
rubrics_metrics.description: In prescribing rules for IPR, PGR, and CBM reviews, the Director must consider the effect of the rules on the economy, the integrity of the patent system, the efficient administration of the Office, and the ability of the Office to complete instituted proceedings in a timely fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory mandate (35 U.S.C. 316(b) and 326(b)) requires balancing policy/economic impacts and administrative capacity when setting procedural rules and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional patent owner preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining whether to institute a review, the patent owner may file an optional patent owner preliminary response to the petition; the patent owner is not required to file a preliminary response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures for filing a preliminary response are set forth in numerous sections (e.g., §§ 42.6, 42.8, 42.11, 42.13, 42.21, 42.23, 42.24(b), 42.51, 42.52, 42.53, 42.54, 42.63, 42.64, 42.65, 42.107, 42.120, 42.207, 42.220). Filing a preliminary response can affect institution decisions and strategy, particularly near statutory time bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution decision timing (three-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will determine whether to institute a trial within three months after the earlier of: (1) the submission of a patent owner preliminary response, (2) waiver of filing a patent owner preliminary response, or (3) expiration of the time period for filing a patent owner preliminary response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Office decides not to institute a trial, the petitioner may file a request for reconsideration. This three-month institution-decision target is a key procedural deadline for petitioners and patent owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a petition to institute review
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is not the owner of a patent may file a petition to institute a review of that patent, with a few statutory exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners need not be patent owners; in practice petitions are often filed by entities practicing in the same or a similar field. CBM reviews are limited to covered business method patents that are not patents for technological inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory time-bar considerations for petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions are subject to statutory time periods (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 315(b) and 325(b)); filing a petition close to expiration of the applicable time bar can affect whether a patent owner benefits from filing a successful preliminary response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing relative to the one-year bars and other statutory deadlines is a strategic and jurisdictional consideration; parties should track these deadlines carefully when preparing petitions or deciding whether to file preliminary responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner qualifications and pro hac vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The skills necessary to prepare a petition or participate in a trial are typically possessed by a registered patent practitioner with experience in the practice area; where authorized by the Board, a non-registered practitioner may be admitted pro hac vice on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparing and litigating IPR/PGR/CBM proceedings generally requires experienced patent attorneys/agents; pro hac vice admission is discretionary and depends on facts/circumstances and practitioner skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties can agree to certain procedural changes without Board motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules adopt changes permitting parties to agree to certain changes from the default process between themselves without filing a motion with the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the need for some contested motions and allows procedural efficiency by mutual agreement, subject to any limits in the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions, oppositions, and replies procedures and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules set procedures for filing motions, oppositions, and replies (various §§ listed); the Office expects an average of 6 motions/oppositions/replies per IPR trial after institution and 8 per PGR/CBM trial after institution, with many motions decided via conference call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific procedural sections include §§ 42.6, 42.8, 42.11, 42.13, 42.21, 42.22, 42.24(a)(5), 42.51–42.54, 42.63–42.65, and others; settlements reduce the number of motions filed in a given trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing requests
rubrics_metrics.description: After a trial has been instituted but prior to a final written decision, parties may request an oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure for filing requests for oral argument is set forth in § 42.70. The Office estimates costs and expects a substantial number of requests for oral hearings; oral hearings may increase complexity and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement confidentiality and adverse judgment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may file requests to treat settlements as business confidential, requests for adverse judgment, and written requests to make settlement agreements available; procedures for these filings are set out in specific sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures and sections: treat settlement as business confidential (§ 42.74(c)), requests for adverse judgment (§ 42.73(b)), and making a settlement available (§ 42.74(c)(2)). Given short trial timelines, ADR options may be infrequently used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee structure (claims-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees for filing petitions depend on the type of review and the number of claims challenged: for IPR, $27,200 to review 20 or fewer claims and $600 per claim in excess of 20; for PGR/CBM, $35,800 to review 20 or fewer claims and $800 per claim in excess of 20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees are set to recover the aggregate cost of providing the review (judge time, support, indirect costs). An IT-component fee is included (see next rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: IT component fee in petition fees
rubrics_metrics.description: An IT component is included in petition fees: base $1,705 for requests to review 20 or fewer claims and $75 per claim in excess of 20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IT component recovers estimated IT setup and maintenance costs through a defined horizon (e.g., through 2017 in the analysis). The remainder of the petition fee recovers judge and indirect costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge time estimates used for fee calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated judge time per petition: for IPR (20 or fewer challenged claims) about 100 hours of judge time plus ~2 hours per claim in excess of 20; for PGR/CBM (20 or fewer challenged claims) about 130 hours plus slightly less than 3 hours per claim in excess of 20. Fully burdened judge cost per hour estimated at $258.32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These time and cost estimates underpin the fee-setting methodology and indicate the expected administrative burden per instituted review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated professional preparation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated outside professional costs: preparing an IPR petition ~ $46,000; preparing a PGR/CBM petition ~ 33.333% higher (~$61,333); patent owner preliminary response estimated 91.6 hours costing ~$34,000; request for reconsideration ~80 hours costing ~$29,680.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates are informed by AIPLA survey data and are intended to help stakeholders anticipate non-Office costs associated with filings and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small entity size standard for USPTO RFA purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: For USPTO Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses, the Office uses an alternate small entity size standard based on 13 CFR 121.802: an entity whose number of employees (including affiliates) does not exceed 500 persons and which has not assigned/licensed rights to a non-qualifying concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This USPTO-specific small-entity standard (distinct from the SBA's industry-specific standards) determines eligibility for reduced patent fees and is used in economic impact estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable procedural sections for petitions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners and patent owners should consult the listed sections to determine precise procedural requirements, filing contents, timing, and subsequent trial rules.
